title: TESS eclipse times show a 1.6-year near-coplanar third body in HD 303514; three-body fits that also match 2002-2008 ASAS-3 depths predict no eclipse loss before 2060
abstract: HD 303514 is a detached 19.897-day eclipsing binary whose eclipses became shallower from 2002 to 2026. Earlier SCI work predicted that the eclipses stop near 2030-2032, with an assumed, undetected third body. We made our own aperture photometry from TESS cutouts of 8 sectors (2019-2026) and measured 18 eclipse times (errors 2.6-14 min from residual permutation). The times deviate from a linear ephemeris by -58 to +62 minutes, with primary and secondary eclipses moving together (chi-square 651 for a linear ephemeris, 26.8 with one 583-day sinusoid). The result does not change with aperture, fit window or eclipse model. Newtonian three-body fits (REBOUND IAS15, light-travel time included) of the times and of sector impact parameters from twin-star eclipse fits give an outer period of 584-600 days (P2/P1 = 30) and e2 = 0.2-0.4. The signal is mainly the dynamical delay. TESS-only fits give a near-coplanar and a near-polar family. Without refitting, the near-coplanar solution predicts the six ASAS-3 depths of 2002-2008 with one V-band light fraction (chi-square 1.5). The near-polar solution needs a light fraction above 1 and has Kozai-Lidov cycles to inner eccentricity 0.999, so we reject it. A joint fit gives mutual inclinations of 3-8 deg. The third-body mass has a lower limit, m3/M12 >= about 0.3 (m3 <= 0.8 solar masses for M12 = 4 is worse by chi-square >= 9.8), and no dynamical upper limit. One main-sequence third star agrees with the fitted light fraction only for m3 = 1.2-1.8 solar masses, which is worse than the best fit by 3.3-6.4 in chi-square. A heavier third body would have to be underluminous, for example a close pair. In all fitted solutions the nodal precession turns the orbit before contact is lost: the impact parameter reaches 1.88-1.95 (primary) and 1.92-1.98 (secondary) stellar radii, below the loss limit of 2, between 2028 and 2034. The eclipses then deepen again. This contradicts the earlier eclipse-loss forecast. We give eclipse-time predictions for 2026-2027 that TESS can test. Limits: a twin-star eclipse model whose systematic errors are comparable to the predicted margin to eclipse loss; aggregate ASAS-3 depths from earlier work; local fits rather than a global posterior; no spectroscopy.
